questions.q: What does `WITH RECOVERY` do when restoring a database?
options: Finalizes the restore, rolls back uncommitted transactions, and brings the database online — no further backups can be applied afterward
Leaves the database in a RESTORING state so more backups can be applied
Deletes the backup file after restoring it
Compresses the restored database automatically
questions.explain: WITH RECOVERY is the terminal step of a restore chain — once applied, the database is online and no additional backups can be layered on top.

questions.q: Why would a DBA use `WITH NORECOVERY` instead of `WITH RECOVERY` when restoring a full backup?
options: Because more backups (a differential or log backups) still need to be applied before the restore is complete
Because NORECOVERY restores faster than RECOVERY
Because NORECOVERY is required for every restore regardless of scenario
Because NORECOVERY automatically applies the next backup in sequence
questions.explain: NORECOVERY leaves the database in a RESTORING state specifically so additional backups in the chain can still be restored on top.

questions.q: What happens if you try to restore a backup over an existing database of the same name without `WITH REPLACE`?
options: SQL Server refuses the restore as a safety check against overwriting an unrelated database
SQL Server silently overwrites the existing database
SQL Server renames the existing database automatically
SQL Server merges the two databases together
questions.explain: WITH REPLACE is a deliberate safety check — without it, SQL Server won't overwrite a database whose backup history doesn't match what's being restored.

questions.q: What do `RESTORE HEADERONLY` and `RESTORE FILELISTONLY` have in common?
options: Both are read-only commands that inspect a backup file without touching the target database
Both permanently modify the backup file
Both are required before any RESTORE DATABASE command
Both bring a database online
questions.explain: HEADERONLY lists the backup sets in a file, and FILELISTONLY lists the logical/physical files it expects — both are diagnostic, read-only checks against the backup file itself.

questions.q: A DBA restores a full backup WITH RECOVERY, then realizes a differential backup taken later that day should also have been applied. What must they do?
options: Start the restore over from the full backup, this time using WITH NORECOVERY, so the differential can then be applied
Restore just the differential backup on top of the already-recovered database
Nothing — the differential will apply automatically
Rename the database and restore the differential into the new name
questions.explain: Once a database is recovered, it can't accept more backups. The only fix is restoring the full backup again with NORECOVERY, then applying the differential.
